payload.throughline: Account for reaction energy, combine enthalpy and entropy to determine direction, then separate equilibrium position from reaction rate.

Objective: Compute a reaction enthalpy by preserving signs and stoichiometric scaling across thermochemical equations or by inventorying bonds broken and formed.
Use the prior thermodynamic-system and First-Law work from the prerequisite sequence: energy is accounted for at a stated system boundary, and enthalpy is a state function.
For a thermochemical equation, a negative reaction enthalpy means the written reaction releases heat at constant pressure; a positive value means it absorbs heat.
Hess’s law works because enthalpy depends on initial and final states. Reverse an equation and reverse its enthalpy sign; multiply every coefficient and multiply its enthalpy by the same factor.
When only average bond energies are supplied, estimate reaction enthalpy as the energy required to break reactant bonds minus the energy released when product bonds form.

Treat reaction enthalpy as an energy ledger: transform whole equations, cancel intermediates, and total the signed entries. For bond data, make two explicit inventories—broken and formed—before subtracting.

I first inspect the data type. Complete thermochemical equations call for a Hess combination; a list of average bond energies calls for a bond inventory. I do not mix the two methods or use activation energy as reaction enthalpy.
Suppose A → B has ΔH = +32 kJ/mol and B → C has ΔH = −50 kJ/mol. Adding the equations cancels B, so A → C has ΔH = −18 kJ/mol.
If the target instead required C → A, I would reverse the net equation and report +18 kJ/mol. The direction of the written reaction controls the sign.
Guided attempt: identify what changed in the written thermochemical equation before touching the enthalpy value.
Less support: transform and combine two equations, keeping a signed ledger.
Independent practice: choose the appropriate enthalpy method from the supplied data.

Boundary: activation energy describes the barrier along a pathway, not the energy difference between products and reactants. A catalyst can lower that barrier while leaving reaction enthalpy unchanged.

Repair the Hess function with a cancellation ledger. Write the target species and side, reverse any equation needed to place an intermediate on the opposite side, scale all coefficients, then add only after the intermediate cancels.

Repair the bond-energy function with two columns. Count every bond broken in reactants, count every bond formed in products, total each column, and compute broken minus formed.

Enthalpy accounting is direction-sensitive and stoichiometry-sensitive: reverse flips the sign, scaling multiplies the value, and bond estimates use broken minus formed.

Objective: Relate enthalpy and entropy through ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, preserve units and signs, and predict the spontaneous direction under stated conditions.
Use the prior lesson’s system boundary, temperature, and entropy-direction reasoning. This lesson combines those quantities into a free-energy criterion rather than reteaching their full foundations.
At constant temperature and pressure, a negative ΔG supports the forward process as thermodynamically spontaneous under the stated conditions; a positive ΔG supports the reverse direction.
In ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, temperature is in kelvin and ΔH and TΔS must use the same energy units. Convert joules to kilojoules when needed before combining terms.
Sign pairs give a useful temperature map: ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0 is favorable at all temperatures; ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0 is unfavorable at all temperatures. Same-sign pairs depend on temperature.
Picture an enthalpy–entropy balance. The ΔH term keeps its sign; the entropy contribution enters as −TΔS and grows in magnitude as temperature rises.

I decide whether a sign-only prediction is sufficient. If the signs settle the result, I do not invent numbers. If temperature can change the result, I either calculate ΔG or find the crossover after matching units.
For ΔH = +30 kJ/mol and ΔS = +120 J/(mol·K), convert ΔS to 0.120 kJ/(mol·K). At 350 K, ΔG = 30 − 350(0.120) = −12 kJ/mol.
The positive entropy term wins at this temperature, so the forward process is thermodynamically favored even though it is endothermic.
Guided attempt: preserve the minus sign on TΔS and convert entropy units before calculating.
Less support: classify the sign pair before deciding whether temperature matters.
Independent practice: determine a temperature condition for spontaneity.
Boundary: spontaneous does not mean rapid. ΔG describes thermodynamic direction under stated conditions; activation energy and rate constants describe how quickly the system approaches change.

Objective: Use ΔG° = −RT ln K to relate equilibrium position to standard free energy while keeping equilibrium position distinct from reaction rate.
Use the prerequisite sequence’s equilibrium constants, reaction-energy profiles, and catalyst effects. Here those ideas are coordinated with standard free energy rather than rederived.
At a fixed positive temperature, ΔG° = −RT ln K. If K > 1, ln K is positive and ΔG° is negative; if K < 1, ln K is negative and ΔG° is positive.
K describes the equilibrium composition for the written reaction under stated conditions. It does not report how rapidly equilibrium is reached.
A catalyst lowers activation barriers for forward and reverse pathways. It can change both rate constants while leaving their ratio—and therefore K at that temperature—unchanged.

Use a two-axis model: the vertical reactant-to-product free-energy difference sets equilibrium position, while the pathway barrier sets rate. A catalyst changes the barrier axis, not the endpoint difference.

I ask whether the prompt changes endpoint thermodynamics or pathway kinetics. A changed K or ΔG° concerns equilibrium position; a changed activation barrier or paired rate constants concerns approach speed.
At a fixed temperature, K = 25 gives ln K > 0, so −RT ln K is negative. Products are favored at equilibrium for the reaction as written.
Adding a catalyst may make the equilibrium mixture appear sooner, but the same temperature and endpoint states mean the equilibrium constant is unchanged.
Guided attempt: use the sign of ln K before considering any numerical logarithm.
Less support: translate between K relative to one and the sign of ΔG°.
Independent practice: separate a kinetic intervention from an equilibrium-position claim.
Boundary: a larger forward rate constant alone does not prove a larger equilibrium constant unless the reverse rate constant and mechanism context are also accounted for.
Near-use exit: apply the practiced function to new values without answer-bearing support.
Changed-task exit: preserve the knowledge component while selecting the operation in a substantively different situation.
Repair the K–ΔG° sign function by writing the sign of ln K first. Because R and T are positive and the equation has a leading minus sign, ΔG° has the opposite sign.

K and ΔG° encode equilibrium position with opposite sign logic; activation barriers and rate constants encode speed. Catalysts change speed, not the equilibrium endpoint.
